title: NORCET — Medical Surgical Nursing | Hemophilia
description: Subject-wise test on Hemophilia (Medical Surgical Nursing) for NORCET. 40Q.

questions.question: What is the most common type of hemophilia, accounting for approximately 80% of all cases?

options.explanation: Hemophilia B accounts for 15-20% of cases and is caused by a deficiency in Factor IX.
Hemophilia A is the most common type, accounting for 80% of cases, caused by a deficiency in Factor VIII.
Hemophilia C is rare and caused by a deficiency in Factor XI.
Von Willebrand Disease is a separate bleeding disorder involving von Willebrand factor.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A, also known as classic hemophilia, is caused by a deficiency in Factor VIII and is the most prevalent form of the disorder, affecting about 1 in 5,000 male births. Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) accounts for about 15-20% of cases, while Hemophilia C (Factor XI deficiency) is rarer and typically milder. Von Willebrand Disease is a separate bleeding disorder involving von Willebrand factor.
questions.hint: Consider the prevalence and the factor deficiency associated with each type.

questions.question: Which of the following laboratory coagulation tests is typically prolonged in a patient with Hemophilia A or B, while the others remain normal?

options.explanation: PT measures the extrinsic pathway and is typically normal in hemophilia.
Bleeding time assesses platelet function and vascular integrity, and is normal in hemophilia.
aPTT assesses the intrinsic and common pathways and is prolonged in hemophilia due to Factor VIII or IX deficiency.
Platelet count measures platelet quantity and is normal in hemophilia.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia involves a deficiency in Factor VIII (Hemophilia A) or Factor IX (Hemophilia B), both of which are part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway. The activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) specifically assesses the intrinsic and common pathways, thus it will be prolonged. The Prothrombin Time (PT) measures the extrinsic pathway and is typically normal. Bleeding time assesses platelet function and vascular integrity, and platelet count measures platelet quantity; both are normal in hemophilia.
questions.hint: Recall the pathways involved in coagulation and which factors are deficient in hemophilia.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with severe Hemophilia A falls from his bicycle and develops a swollen, painful right knee (hemarthrosis). What is the nurse's immediate priority intervention?

options.text: Administer Factor VIII replacement therapy immediately.
options.explanation: Factor VIII replacement is the immediate priority to control bleeding and prevent joint damage in a patient with severe Hemophilia A.

options.text: Apply a cold compress to the knee and elevate the limb.
options.explanation: While RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) may help with pain and swelling, it does not address the underlying bleeding disorder.

options.text: Perform a joint aspiration to relieve pressure and pain.
options.explanation: Joint aspiration is contraindicated in hemophilia due to the risk of exacerbating bleeding and introducing infection.

options.text: Administer nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain relief.
options.explanation: NSAIDs should be avoided in hemophilia as they can increase bleeding risk by inhibiting platelet function.

questions.explanation: In a patient with hemophilia experiencing hemarthrosis, the immediate priority is to prevent further joint damage and control bleeding. Factor VIII replacement therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for Hemophilia A to restore clotting factor levels. Rest, ice, compression, and elevation (RICE) may be used adjunctively, but factor replacement is critical.
questions.hint: Consider the pathophysiology of hemophilia and the immediate need to address the bleeding episode.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: Which coagulation factor deficiency is characteristic of Hemophilia A?

options.explanation: Factor IX deficiency is characteristic of Hemophilia B.
Factor VII is part of the extrinsic pathway and not associated with Hemophilia A.
Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency in Factor VIII.
Factor X is part of the common pathway and not associated with Hemophilia A.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A, also known as classic hemophilia, is caused by a deficiency or defect in coagulation Factor VIII. Hemophilia B is due to Factor IX deficiency, and Factor VII and X are part of the extrinsic pathway and common pathway respectively.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: Hemophilia A and B are inherited in which of the following patterns?

options.explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders require only one copy of the affected gene to manifest the disease, which is not the case for hemophilia.
Hemophilia A and B are inherited as X-linked recessive traits.
Autosomal recessive disorders require two copies of the affected gene, which is not the inheritance pattern for hemophilia.
X-linked dominant disorders are rare and do not apply to hemophilia.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A and B are both X-linked recessive disorders. This means that the gene responsible for the condition is located on the X chromosome, and a male needs only one copy of the affected gene to develop the disorder, while females are typically carriers.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with spontaneous bleeding into his knee joint (hemarthrosis). Lab tests show a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), a normal prothrombin time (PT), and a normal platelet count. These findings are most consistent with:

options.explanation: ITP presents with a low platelet count, which is not seen in this case.
vWD can have a prolonged aPTT but often also prolonged bleeding time and abnormal von Willebrand factor levels.
The lab findings are consistent with hemophilia, indicating a defect in the intrinsic coagulation pathway.
DIC typically presents with prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelet count, and elevated D-dimer.

questions.explanation: Prolonged aPTT, normal PT, and normal platelet count are classic laboratory findings for hemophilia, indicating a defect in the intrinsic coagulation pathway (Factors VIII or IX). ITP would show a low platelet count. vWD can have a prolonged aPTT but often also prolonged bleeding time and abnormal von Willebrand factor levels. DIC typically presents with prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelet count, and elevated D-dimer.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a child with Hemophilia A who experiences an acute hemarthrosis in his elbow. What is the priority nursing intervention?

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the joint.
options.explanation: Warm compresses are contraindicated as they can increase bleeding.

options.text: Encourage active range of motion exercises.
options.explanation: Active range of motion is contraindicated during an acute bleed to avoid further injury.

options.text: Administer factor replacement therapy as prescribed.
options.explanation: Administering the deficient factor is the priority to stop the bleeding.

options.text: Elevate the affected joint and encourage weight-bearing.
options.explanation: Elevation is a supportive measure but secondary to factor replacement.

questions.explanation: The priority in managing acute hemarthrosis in hemophilia is to stop the bleeding by administering the deficient factor (Factor VIII for Hemophilia A). This prevents further joint damage. Warm compresses are contraindicated as they can increase bleeding. Active range of motion and weight-bearing are contraindicated during an acute bleed to avoid further injury and pain. Elevation and rest (RICE) are supportive measures but secondary to factor replacement.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analog of vasopressin that can be used in the management of certain bleeding disorders. For which type of hemophilia is DDAVP most likely to be effective?

options.explanation: DDAVP is not effective in severe Hemophilia A due to very low or absent Factor VIII stores.
DDAVP is effective in mild Hemophilia A as it stimulates the release of residual Factor VIII.
DDAVP is not effective in Hemophilia B, which involves Factor IX deficiency.
Hemophilia C is not a commonly recognized type of hemophilia.

questions.explanation: DDAVP works by stimulating the release of stored Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from endothelial cells. It is effective in patients with mild Hemophilia A because they have some residual Factor VIII that can be released. It is generally not effective in severe Hemophilia A (due to very low or absent Factor VIII stores) or Hemophilia B (which involves Factor IX deficiency).
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A patient with severe Hemophilia A develops an inhibitor to Factor VIII. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment strategy for a bleeding episode in this patient?

options.explanation: High-dose recombinant Factor VIII is ineffective in the presence of an inhibitor.
DDAVP is ineffective in the presence of an inhibitor.

options.text: Bypass agents like activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC) or recombinant Factor VIIa.
options.explanation: Bypass agents are used to promote coagulation through alternative routes when Factor VIII inhibitors are present.
Platelet transfusions are not indicated for factor deficiencies.

questions.explanation: When a patient with Hemophilia A develops an inhibitor (antibodies) to Factor VIII, administering Factor VIII concentrate becomes ineffective as the inhibitor neutralizes it. DDAVP is also ineffective as it relies on stimulating the release of Factor VIII. Bypass agents such as activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC) or recombinant Factor VIIa are used to circumvent the Factor VIII pathway and promote coagulation through alternative routes. Platelet transfusions are not indicated for factor deficiencies.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with Hemophilia A falls and hits his head. He is alert but complains of a mild headache. What is the immediate priority for the nurse?

options.explanation: Pain medication is secondary to stopping the bleeding.
Monitoring is important but not the immediate priority.
Immediate factor replacement is critical to prevent intracranial hemorrhage.

options.text: Prepare for a CT scan of the head.
options.explanation: A CT scan is important but secondary to factor replacement.

questions.explanation: Any head injury in a patient with hemophilia is a medical emergency due to the high risk of intracranial hemorrhage, which can be life-threatening. Immediate administration of Factor VIII concentrate is crucial to prevent or minimize bleeding, even if symptoms are mild. While monitoring vital signs, pain management, and a CT scan are important, factor replacement is the most time-critical therapeutic intervention to prevent catastrophic bleeding.

questions.question: A nurse is providing discharge education to parents of a newborn diagnosed with Hemophilia B. Which instruction is most crucial for preventing complications?

options.text: Encourage participation in contact sports to strengthen joints.
options.explanation: Contact sports should be avoided to prevent bleeding.

options.text: Administer aspirin for fever or pain relief.
options.explanation: Aspirin is contraindicated due to its effect on platelet function.
IM injections pose a high risk for hematomas in hemophilia.

options.text: Monitor for signs of increased urination.
options.explanation: Monitoring urination is not a primary preventative measure.

questions.explanation: Intramuscular (IM) injections are a significant risk for deep muscle hematomas in individuals with hemophilia due to bleeding into the muscle. Subcutaneous or intravenous routes are preferred. Contact sports should be avoided. Aspirin and other NSAIDs that impair platelet function are contraindicated. Monitoring urination is not a primary preventative measure for general complications of hemophilia.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common site of spontaneous bleeding in individuals with Hemophilia?

options.explanation: While bleeding can occur in the gastrointestinal tract, it is not the most common site.
Skin bleeding is not characteristic of hemophilia.
Hemarthrosis is the most common and characteristic site of bleeding in hemophilia.
Hematuria can occur but is not the most common site.

questions.explanation: Hemarthrosis, or bleeding into the joints, is the hallmark and most frequent site of spontaneous bleeding in individuals with hemophilia. Repeated hemarthrosis leads to chronic arthropathy. While bleeding can occur in other sites, joint bleeding is the most characteristic and common.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male with a history of Hemophilia A presents with prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. His lab results show: aPTT 70 seconds (normal 25-35), PT 12 seconds (normal 11-13), Platelets 250,000/µL (normal 150-450,000). Which additional test would be most useful to confirm the diagnosis of Hemophilia A?

options.explanation: Factor IX assay would be relevant for Hemophilia B, not Hemophilia A.
Factor VIII assay measures the activity level of Factor VIII, which is deficient in Hemophilia A.
Von Willebrand factor levels are not diagnostic for Hemophilia A.
Bleeding time is not diagnostic for Hemophilia A.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is diagnosed by measuring Factor VIII activity levels. A low Factor VIII level confirms the diagnosis. The aPTT is prolonged due to the intrinsic pathway defect, but Factor VIII assay is the definitive test.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the inheritance pattern of Hemophilia A?

options.explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders are caused by a defective gene on an autosome, and only one copy of the gene is needed to express the disease. Hemophilia A is not inherited this way.
Autosomal recessive disorders require two copies of the defective gene for the disease to manifest. Hemophilia A is not inherited this way.
Hemophilia A is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, where the defective gene is on the X chromosome.
X-linked dominant disorders require only one copy of the defective gene on the X chromosome to express the disease. Hemophilia A is not inherited this way.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A and B are classic examples of X-linked recessive disorders, meaning the gene responsible for the condition is located on the X chromosome, and a male needs only one copy of the defective gene to express the disease, while females are typically carriers.
questions.hint: Consider the chromosome involved and the gender most commonly affected.

questions.question: Hemophilia B, also known as Christmas disease, is characterized by a deficiency of which specific coagulation factor?

options.explanation: Factor VIII deficiency is associated with Hemophilia A, not Hemophilia B.
Hemophilia B is caused by a deficiency in Factor IX.
Factor XI deficiency is associated with a rare bleeding disorder called Hemophilia C, not Hemophilia B.
Factor XII deficiency is not typically associated with significant bleeding symptoms, and it is not linked to Hemophilia B.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia B results from a deficiency or defect in Factor IX, which is essential for the intrinsic coagulation pathway. Hemophilia A involves Factor VIII deficiency.
questions.hint: Recall the specific factor associated with Hemophilia B.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with severe Hemophilia A presents to the emergency department with acute pain and swelling in his right knee after falling during play. What is the immediate priority nursing intervention?

options.explanation: While pain management is important, stopping the bleeding is the immediate priority to prevent further damage.

options.text: Apply a cold compress to the affected joint
options.explanation: Cold compresses can help reduce swelling and pain but do not address the underlying bleeding.
Initiating Factor VIII replacement therapy is the immediate priority to stop the bleeding and prevent joint damage.
Joint aspiration may be considered later if needed, but the priority is to stop the bleeding first.

questions.explanation: The immediate priority in managing acute hemarthrosis in a patient with hemophilia is to stop the bleeding by administering the deficient coagulation factor (Factor VIII in Hemophilia A). This prevents further joint damage and reduces pain. Pain management, cold compresses, and joint aspiration are supportive or secondary measures.
questions.hint: Think about the primary goal in managing acute bleeding episodes in hemophilia.

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing the coagulation profile of a patient diagnosed with Hemophilia A. Which of the following laboratory findings would be characteristic of this condition?

options.text: Prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT), normal Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
options.explanation: PT measures the extrinsic pathway, which is unaffected in Hemophilia A.
Hemophilia A affects the intrinsic pathway, leading to a prolonged aPTT, while PT remains normal.
PT is unaffected in Hemophilia A and should remain normal.

options.text: Normal PT, normal aPTT, prolonged bleeding time
options.explanation: Bleeding time is typically normal in Hemophilia A as platelet function is intact.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of Factor VIII, which is part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway. The aPTT measures the integrity of the intrinsic and common pathways, thus it will be prolonged. The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways, which are unaffected in hemophilia, so it remains normal. Bleeding time, which assesses platelet function, is also normal.
questions.hint: Recall the pathways involved in coagulation and the tests used to evaluate them.

questions.question: A patient with Hemophilia A is scheduled for a dental extraction. What prophylactic measure is most important for the nurse to anticipate and prepare for prior to the procedure?

options.explanation: Tranexamic acid can be used as an adjunct but is not the primary prophylactic measure.

options.text: Pre-procedure administration of Factor VIII concentrate
options.explanation: Prophylactic Factor VIII concentrate is the most important measure to prevent bleeding during the procedure.
Local pressure is a supportive measure post-extraction but does not prevent bleeding during the procedure.

options.text: Availability of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) on standby
options.explanation: FFP contains all factors but is less concentrated and carries more risks than specific factor concentrates.

questions.explanation: For invasive procedures like dental extractions in patients with hemophilia, prophylactic administration of the deficient factor concentrate (Factor VIII for Hemophilia A) is crucial to raise factor levels and prevent excessive bleeding. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and can be used as an adjunct, but not as the primary prophylactic measure. FFP contains all factors but is less concentrated and carries more risks than specific factor concentrates. Local pressure is a general post-procedure measure.
questions.hint: Consider the primary intervention to prevent bleeding during an invasive procedure in a patient with hemophilia.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male with severe Hemophilia B has a history of frequent hemarthroses, primarily affecting his knees and elbows. Which long-term complication is he most at risk for developing?

options.explanation: Osteoporosis is not a direct complication of hemophilia.
Cholelithiasis (gallstones) may occur due to frequent transfusions or liver disease but is not a primary complication of hemophilic arthropathy.
Chronic hemarthrosis leads to hemophilic arthropathy, a long-term complication.
Renal failure is not a typical long-term complication of hemophilia, though it can occur in rare cases due to other factors.

questions.explanation: Recurrent bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) is the hallmark complication of hemophilia. Over time, chronic inflammation, synovial hypertrophy, cartilage destruction, and bone erosion lead to irreversible joint damage, known as hemophilic arthropathy.
questions.hint: Consider the long-term effects of recurrent bleeding into joints.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with easy bruising, epistaxis, and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. His laboratory results show: PT normal, aPTT prolonged, bleeding time prolonged, Factor VIII activity 30% (normal range 50-150%), and von Willebrand factor antigen (vWF:Ag) 25% (normal range 50-150%). Which condition is most likely indicated?

options.explanation: Severe Hemophilia A would show Factor VIII activity <1%, normal bleeding time, and normal vWF levels.
Mild Hemophilia B would show reduced Factor IX levels, not Factor VIII or vWF.
Type 1 vWD presents with mild to moderate Factor VIII deficiency due to vWF stabilizing Factor VIII, prolonged bleeding time, and reduced vWF levels.
DIC typically presents with prolonged PT, aPTT, and thrombocytopenia, which are not seen in this case.

questions.explanation: The combination of prolonged aPTT, prolonged bleeding time, and reduced levels of both Factor VIII and von Willebrand Factor (vWF) is characteristic of von Willebrand Disease (vWD). In severe Hemophilia A, Factor VIII would be significantly lower (<1%), and bleeding time and vWF would be normal. Mild Hemophilia B would show reduced Factor IX, not Factor VIII or vWF. DIC would typically present with prolonged PT, aPTT, and thrombocytopenia.
questions.hint: Consider the combination of laboratory findings and clinical presentation to differentiate between bleeding disorders.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A 40 kg patient with Hemophilia A (baseline Factor VIII level <1%) experiences a significant gastrointestinal bleed. The target Factor VIII level to achieve hemostasis for severe bleeding is 80-100%. Given that 1 unit/kg of Factor VIII typically raises the plasma Factor VIII level by 2%, what is the approximate initial dose of Factor VIII concentrate (in units) required to reach a target of 90%?

options.explanation: 1800 units is the calculated dose needed to achieve a 90% Factor VIII level in a 40 kg patient.
2700 units would be excessive for this scenario.
3600 units is more than needed for this patient.
4500 units is significantly higher than the required dose.

questions.explanation: To calculate the dose: Desired increase in Factor VIII level = Target 90% - Baseline <1% ≈ 90%. Units per kg needed = (90% / 2%) = 45 units/kg. Total dose = 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units.
questions.hint: Use the formula: (Desired increase in Factor VIII level / 2%) * weight in kg = total units required.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A patient with Hemophilia A weighing 40 kg requires Factor VIII replacement therapy. Calculate the total units of Factor VIII required if the prescribed dose is 45 units/kg.

options.explanation: This is incorrect because 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units, not 1600 units.
This is correct because 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units.
This is incorrect because 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units, not 2000 units.
This is incorrect because 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units, not 2200 units.

questions.explanation: The total units of Factor VIII required are calculated by multiplying the dose per kg (45 units/kg) by the patient's weight (40 kg). Thus, 45 units/kg * 40 kg = 1800 units.
questions.hint: Multiply the dose per kg by the patient's weight to get the total units.

questions.question: A patient with severe Hemophilia A previously responded well to Factor VIII replacement therapy but now experiences persistent bleeding despite adequate factor dosing. Laboratory tests confirm the presence of Factor VIII inhibitors. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Increase the dose of Factor VIII
options.explanation: Increasing the dose of Factor VIII is ineffective in patients with inhibitors as the inhibitors neutralize the administered Factor VIII.
Desmopressin is not effective in patients with severe Hemophilia A or those with inhibitors as it primarily releases endogenous Factor VIII, which is absent or inhibited in these patients.

options.text: Use a bypassing agent like activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC) or recombinant activated Factor VII (rFVIIa)
options.explanation: Bypassing agents such as aPCC or rFVIIa are the most appropriate initial treatments as they bypass the need for Factor VIII by directly activating the coagulation cascade.
Fresh frozen plasma contains Factor VIII but is ineffective in the presence of inhibitors and may lead to fluid overload.

questions.explanation: The presence of Factor VIII inhibitors indicates an immune response against Factor VIII, rendering standard replacement therapy ineffective. The most appropriate initial treatment is to bypass the inhibitor using a bypassing agent such as activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC) or recombinant activated Factor VII (rFVIIa).
questions.hint: Consider treatments that bypass the need for Factor VIII due to the presence of inhibitors.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A 5-year-old male child is brought to the emergency department with a history of spontaneous bleeding into the left knee joint. On examination, the knee is swollen, warm, and tender. The child has a positive family history of bleeding disorders. Which laboratory finding is most consistent with the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Prolonged bleeding time and normal platelet count
options.explanation: Bleeding time is normal in hemophilia as platelet function is intact.

options.text: Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and normal prothrombin time (PT)
options.explanation: Prolonged aPTT is consistent with hemophilia due to deficiency in intrinsic pathway clotting factors (VIII or IX).
Prolonged PT indicates an issue with the extrinsic pathway, which is not typical in hemophilia.

options.text: Prolonged thrombin time and low fibrinogen level
options.explanation: Thrombin time and fibrinogen levels are typically normal in hemophilia unless complicated by DIC.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia is characterized by a deficiency in clotting factors, primarily Factor VIII (Hemophilia A) or Factor IX (Hemophilia B). The intrinsic pathway is affected, leading to a prolonged aPTT, while the PT remains normal. Bleeding time is normal as platelet function is intact. Thrombin time and fibrinogen levels are typically normal unless there is a secondary issue like disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
questions.hint: Consider the intrinsic pathway clotting factors and their associated lab tests.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male with known Hemophilia A is admitted for a scheduled dental extraction. The patient’s baseline Factor VIII level is 2% of normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate pre-procedural management to prevent bleeding?

options.text: Administration of oral tranexamic acid alone
options.explanation: Tranexamic acid is useful as an adjunct but not sufficient alone for major procedures in severe hemophilia.

options.text: Infusion of recombinant Factor VIII to achieve a level of 50–80 IU/dL before the procedure and maintaining it for 7–10 days
options.explanation: Factor VIII replacement to achieve 50–80 IU/dL before and after the procedure is critical for adequate hemostasis.
Vitamin K is not indicated for hemophilia-related bleeding prevention.
Heparin is contraindicated in hemophilia as it increases bleeding risk.

questions.explanation: Patients with severe Hemophilia A (Factor VIII level <1%) require factor replacement therapy to raise the Factor VIII level to 50–80 IU/dL before invasive procedures and maintain it for 7–10 days to ensure adequate hemostasis. Tranexamic acid is useful as an adjunct but not sufficient alone. Vitamin K and heparin are not indicated for hemophilia-related bleeding prevention.
questions.hint: Consider the severity of hemophilia and the need for factor replacement to achieve hemostasis.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with Hemophilia A presents with sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and altered sensorium. CT scan of the brain reveals an intracranial hemorrhage. Which of the following is the immediate priority management step?

options.explanation: Desmopressin is used for mild hemophilia or von Willebrand disease but not for severe hemophilia or major bleeding.

options.text: Immediate infusion of recombinant Factor VIII to achieve a level of 100 IU/dL
options.explanation: Immediate factor replacement to achieve a Factor VIII level of 100 IU/dL is critical to stop bleeding in intracranial hemorrhage.
Platelet transfusion is not indicated for hemophilia A-related bleeding.
Corticosteroids are not indicated for hemophilia A-related bleeding.

questions.explanation: Intracranial hemorrhage in a hemophilia patient is a medical emergency. Immediate factor replacement to achieve a Factor VIII level of 100 IU/dL is critical to stop bleeding. Desmopressin is used for mild hemophilia or von Willebrand disease but not for severe hemophilia or major bleeding. Platelets and steroids are not indicated for hemophilia A-related bleeding.
questions.hint: Consider the life-threatening nature of intracranial hemorrhage and the need for rapid factor replacement.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: Which of the following statements best differentiates Hemophilia A from Hemophilia B?

options.text: Hemophilia A is more common and results from a deficiency of Factor IX, while Hemophilia B results from Factor VIII deficiency
options.explanation: Hemophilia A results from Factor VIII deficiency, not Factor IX.

options.text: Both Hemophilia A and B are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
options.explanation: Both hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders, not autosomal recessive.

options.text: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of Factor VIII and is more common than Hemophilia B
options.explanation: Hemophilia A is caused by Factor VIII deficiency and is more common than Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency).

options.text: Hemophilia B is treated with Factor VIII concentrate, while Hemophilia A requires Factor IX
options.explanation: Hemophilia A is treated with Factor VIII concentrate, while Hemophilia B requires Factor IX.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) is more common than Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency). Both are X-linked recessive disorders, not autosomal recessive. Hemophilia A is treated with Factor VIII concentrate, while Hemophilia B requires Factor IX.
questions.hint: Consider the specific clotting factors involved in each type of hemophilia.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A 30-year-old male with Hemophilia A is on regular prophylactic Factor VIII infusions. He develops a high-titer inhibitor (antibodies against Factor VIII). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to recombinant Factor VIIa for on-demand treatment
options.explanation: Bypassing agents like recombinant Factor VIIa are used to treat bleeding in patients with high-titer inhibitors.

options.text: Increase the dose of Factor VIII to overcome the inhibitor
options.explanation: Increasing Factor VIII dose is ineffective in the presence of inhibitors.
IVIG is not effective in treating factor inhibitors.

options.text: Start long-term antibiotics to prevent infections
options.explanation: Antibiotics are not indicated for management of factor inhibitors.

questions.explanation: High-titer inhibitors neutralize infused Factor VIII, making it ineffective. In such cases, bypassing agents like recombinant Factor VIIa (NovoSeven) or activated prothrombin complex concentrates (FEIBA) are used to achieve hemostasis without requiring Factor VIII. Increasing Factor VIII dose is ineffective in the presence of inhibitors.
questions.hint: Consider the role of inhibitors in neutralizing factor replacement therapy.
questions.subject: norcet-msn

questions.question: A neonate is diagnosed with Hemophilia B after prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern in this case?

options.explanation: Hemophilia is not inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
Hemophilia is not inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
Hemophilia B is an X-linked recessive disorder.
Hemophilia is not inherited in a mitochondrial pattern.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia B, like Hemophilia A, is an X-linked recessive disorder. This means the gene mutation is located on the X chromosome, and males (who have one X chromosome) are typically affected, while females are usually carriers. Autosomal or mitochondrial inheritance patterns do not apply to hemophilia.
questions.hint: Consider the genetic basis of hemophilia.

questions.question: During a routine follow-up, a 15-year-old girl with mild Hemophilia A (Factor VIII level 15%) complains of heavy menstrual bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?

options.text: Oral contraceptive pills to regulate menstrual bleeding
options.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills can help regulate menstrual bleeding and reduce blood loss in mild hemophilia.
Iron supplementation may be needed if anemia develops but does not address the acute bleeding.

options.text: High-dose Factor VIII infusion every month
options.explanation: High-dose Factor VIII is not routinely required for menorrhagia in mild hemophilia.

options.text: Administration of aspirin for pain relief
options.explanation: Aspirin is contraindicated as it inhibits platelet function and worsens bleeding.

questions.explanation: In mild hemophilia, oral contraceptive pills can help regulate menstrual bleeding and reduce blood loss. Iron supplementation may be needed if anemia develops, but it does not address the acute bleeding. High-dose Factor VIII is not routinely required for menorrhagia in mild cases. Aspirin is contraindicated as it inhibits platelet function and worsens bleeding.
questions.hint: Consider hormonal and non-factor replacement options for managing menorrhagia in mild hemophilia.

questions.question: A 40-year-old male with Hemophilia A undergoes a minor surgical procedure. Postoperatively, he develops a wound hematoma. His Factor VIII level is maintained at 50 IU/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment to promote wound healing?

options.explanation: Topical thrombin may help locally but is insufficient for a hematoma.
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that helps stabilize clots and reduce bleeding.
Heparin is contraindicated as it increases bleeding risk.
NSAIDs like ibuprofen are contraindicated as they inhibit platelet function and worsen bleeding.

questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that helps stabilize clots and reduce bleeding. It is commonly used as an adjunct in hemophilia patients to prevent excessive bleeding post-surgery or trauma. Topical thrombin may help locally but is insufficient for a hematoma. Heparin and NSAIDs are contraindicated as they increase bleeding risk.

questions.question: Which of the following diagnostic tests is most useful to differentiate between Hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (vWD) in a patient with a bleeding disorder?

options.explanation: PT is nonspecific for differentiating Hemophilia A and vWD.
aPTT is prolonged in both conditions and is nonspecific for differentiation.

options.text: Factor VIII level and von Willebrand factor (vWF) antigen/activity
options.explanation: Measuring Factor VIII and vWF levels/activity is the definitive test to differentiate Hemophilia A from vWD.
Platelet count and bleeding time may be abnormal in vWD but are not diagnostic.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is characterized by low Factor VIII levels, while vWD involves low von Willebrand factor (vWF) levels or activity. PT and aPTT are nonspecific. Platelet count and bleeding time may be abnormal in vWD but are not diagnostic. Measuring Factor VIII and vWF levels/activity is the definitive test.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male with severe Hemophilia A (Factor VIII <1%) is scheduled for a major orthopedic surgery. What is the target Factor VIII level that should be maintained during the perioperative period to ensure adequate hemostasis?

30–50 IU/dL is sufficient for minor procedures but not major orthopedic surgery.
For major surgeries, the target Factor VIII level is 50–80 IU/dL, maintained for 7–10 days postoperatively.
100–150 IU/dL is used for life-threatening bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage, not routine major orthopedic surgery.

questions.explanation: For major surgeries in patients with severe hemophilia, the target Factor VIII level is 50–80 IU/dL, maintained for 7–10 days postoperatively to ensure adequate hemostasis and wound healing. Lower levels (10–50 IU/dL) are sufficient for minor procedures or minor bleeding. Levels of 100–150 IU/dL are used for life-threatening bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with a known history of severe Hemophilia A presents to the emergency department with acute pain and swelling in his right knee after a minor fall. On examination, the knee is warm, tender, and has a decreased range of motion. What is the most immediate and appropriate nursing intervention?

options.text: Apply ice to the affected joint and elevate the limb.
options.explanation: While supportive, this does not address the immediate need to stop bleeding in hemophilia.

options.text: Prepare for immediate administration of recombinant Factor VIII.
options.explanation: This is the most immediate and appropriate intervention to control bleeding in Hemophilia A.

options.text: Encourage active range of motion exercises to prevent stiffness.
options.explanation: This is contraindicated during an acute bleeding episode as it may worsen the bleed.

options.text: Obtain an immediate X-ray of the knee to rule out fracture.
options.explanation: While important, it is secondary to controlling the bleed.

questions.explanation: In a patient with hemophilia experiencing a bleeding episode (hemarthrosis in this case), the most critical and immediate intervention is to replace the deficient clotting factor. While RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) and pain management are important supportive measures, they do not address the underlying cause of bleeding. An X-ray might be needed later but is secondary to stopping the bleed.

questions.question: A patient with Hemophilia B is undergoing routine coagulation studies. Which of the following laboratory findings would be characteristic of this condition?

options.explanation: PT prolongation is not characteristic of Hemophilia B.
Hemophilia B affects the intrinsic pathway, leading to a prolonged aPTT while PT remains normal.
Only aPTT is prolonged in Hemophilia B; PT is typically normal.

options.text: Normal PT, normal aPTT, and decreased platelet count
options.explanation: Platelet count is typically normal in hemophilia.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) affects the intrinsic pathway of coagulation, which is measured by the Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT). Therefore, a prolonged aPTT is characteristic. The extrinsic pathway, measured by Prothrombin Time (PT), and the platelet count are typically normal in hemophilia.

questions.question: A 28-year-old male with severe Hemophilia A is on a prophylaxis regimen with recombinant Factor VIII. He presents to the clinic with persistent joint pain and recurrent bleeds despite adhering to his prescribed factor replacement schedule. His aPTT remains prolonged even after factor infusion. What is the most likely underlying complication?

options.explanation: Inhibitors neutralize infused Factor VIII, leading to persistent bleeding and prolonged aPTT despite therapy.

options.text: Factor VIII resistance due to genetic mutation
options.explanation: Factor VIII resistance is rare compared to the development of inhibitors.
Vitamin K deficiency affects PT more than aPTT.

options.text: Acute liver failure affecting coagulation factor synthesis
options.explanation: Liver failure would affect multiple coagulation factors, leading to both PT and aPTT prolongation.

questions.explanation: The development of inhibitors (antibodies) against infused Factor VIII is a serious and common complication in patients with severe Hemophilia A, particularly those with recurrent bleeding despite adequate factor replacement. These inhibitors neutralize the administered factor, rendering the treatment ineffective and leading to persistent bleeding and a prolonged aPTT even after infusion. Factor VIII resistance is rare. Vitamin K deficiency primarily affects PT, and liver failure would affect multiple coagulation factors, often leading to both PT and aPTT prolongation.

questions.question: A female carrier of Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) is pregnant with her first child. She asks the nurse about the probability of her child inheriting the condition. What is the correct information the nurse should provide regarding the inheritance pattern and risk?

options.text: There is a 50% chance her son will have Hemophilia B and a 50% chance her daughter will be a carrier.
options.explanation: This correctly describes the inheritance pattern for an X-linked recessive disorder like Hemophilia B.

options.text: All her sons will have Hemophilia B, and all her daughters will be carriers.
options.explanation: This is incorrect; the probability is 50% for each child.

options.text: There is a 25% chance her child (regardless of sex) will have Hemophilia B.
options.explanation: The probability depends on the sex of the child and is not 25%.

options.text: Hemophilia B is autosomal recessive, so neither her sons nor daughters are at risk unless the father also carries the gene.
options.explanation: Hemophilia B is X-linked recessive, not autosomal recessive.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia B is an X-linked recessive disorder. A female carrier has one normal X chromosome and one X chromosome carrying the mutated Factor IX gene. Each time she conceives: There is a 50% chance her son will inherit the mutated X chromosome and thus have Hemophilia B. There is a 50% chance her daughter will inherit the mutated X chromosome and thus be a carrier.
questions.hint: Recall the inheritance pattern of X-linked recessive disorders.
